reason: The sources provide over 20 corroborated claims, including specific measurements of luminosity, distance, and competing scientific theories for the event's origin.
story: In 2015, the automated 'ASAS-SN' survey detected a flash in the southern sky so powerful it redefined cosmic violence. Named ASASSN-15lh, this explosion was 20 times brighter than every star in our Milky Way galaxy combined. At its peak, it blazed with the light of 570 billion suns, releasing more energy in its first few months than our Sun will produce in its entire 10-billion-year life. Scientists were initially baffled; the explosion occurred in a 'dead' galaxy where massive stars aren't supposed to exist. While first classified as the most powerful supernova ever seen, later evidence suggests a darker origin: a supermassive black hole 100 million times the mass of the Sun caught a wandering star. The black hole's gravity 'spaghettified' the star, ripping it apart and creating a flare so bright it pushed the absolute theoretical limits of physics.
angle: ASASSN-15lh was 20 times brighter than all the stars in the Milky Way combined, releasing more energy in weeks than our Sun will in its entire 10-billion-year lifetime.

claims.claim: ASASSN-15lh was discovered in June 2015.
The event was detected by the All Sky Automated Survey for SuperNovae (ASAS-SN).
The discovery project is nicknamed 'assassin' after its acronym.
The explosion was 20 times brighter than the combined light of the entire Milky Way galaxy.
At its peak, the event was roughly 570 to 600 billion times brighter than the Sun.
ASASSN-15lh is located approximately 3.8 billion light-years away from Earth.
It was at least twice as bright as the previous record-holding superluminous supernova.
The event released more energy in its first months than the Sun will radiate in its 10-billion-year lifetime.
If it occurred within our own galaxy, it would be brighter than the full moon and visible during the day.
The explosion reached the extreme theoretical limits for how much energy such an event can produce.
It occurred in a massive, red galaxy with very low star formation rates.
Astronomers initially classified the event as a Type I superluminous supernova.
Later research suggests the event was a tidal disruption of a star by a supermassive black hole.
A tidal disruption event involves a star being ripped apart by extreme gravitational forces.
The black hole explanation requires it to be a rapidly spinning Kerr black hole.
The supermassive black hole is estimated to have a mass of at least 100 million times that of the Sun.
The event showed an unusual rebrightening in ultraviolet light roughly 90 days after its peak.
The light from the explosion lacked signatures of hydrogen and helium.
Detection was made using twin 14-centimeter telescopes located in Chile.
The peak temperature of the event was approximately 20,000 Kelvin.

disputed: Classification as a supernova versus a tidal disruption event. Early analysis identified it as a record-breaking supernova, but later peer-reviewed studies argue it is a black hole destroying a star. The script should mention both theories, focusing on the black hole as the more recent consensus.
